extracted.intended_audience: Citizens/voters of New York considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution; readers of the Federalist essays
extracted.subtask_description: A series of Federalist essays (Hamilton, Publius) arguing for constitutional powers of the national government — especially use of force, militia regulation, and taxation — aimed at persuading New York citizens to ratify the proposed Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of national force in emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: That there may happen cases in which the national government may be necessitated to resort to force, cannot be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergencies such as seditions and insurrections will sometimes arise; when they do, 'there could be no remedy but force.' The text argues this is an inevitable consequence of civil society and advances that denying it is unrealistic. Examples: minor commotions handled by militia; larger insurrections may require different force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must be proportioned to the extent of the mischief (proportionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The means to be employed must be proportioned to the extent of the mischief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disturbance is slight and local, the militia of the residue would be adequate; if pervading a whole State, a different (more regular) force may be unavoidable. Policy should fit means to ends; objections based on fear of national force ignore proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia adequacy for small disturbances
rubrics_metrics.description: If it should be a slight commotion in a small part of a State, the militia of the residue would be adequate to its suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption that citizens would support government if it is generally conducive to prosperity. For localized unrest, reliance on militia is appropriate and likely sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a different (regular) force for large insurrections
rubrics_metrics.description: If the insurrection should pervade a whole State, or a principal part of it, the employment of a different kind of force might become unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Massachusetts and Pennsylvania raising troops. States themselves sometimes needed regular forces (e.g., to attempt reasserting jurisdiction). Therefore the national government may face similar necessities; objections that deny this possibility apply equally to state governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for a single larger union over multiple confederacies
rubrics_metrics.description: A general union is preferable to multiple confederacies because the same difficulties (insurrections, emergencies) would occur in each, but a larger union reduces unceasing agitations and frequent revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: dividing into separate confederacies does not eliminate the need for extraordinary force; a larger union makes popular resistance and mutual support more effective, reducing the scourges of petty republics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government as primary security against abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole power of the proposed government is to be in the hands of the representatives of the people. This is the essential ... security for the rights and privileges of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If representatives betray constituents, the ultimate remedy is self-defense; but representative institutions are presented as the chief, practicable safeguard against national usurpation — more effective than peremptory prohibitions against military establishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of territory increases obstacles to usurpation and facilities of resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The obstacles to usurpation and the facilities of resistance increase with the increased extent of the state, provided the citizens understand their rights and are disposed to defend them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a large community the people's natural strength relative to artificial government strength is greater; in a confederacy multiple governments check one another; distant states can provide fresh forces if one is subdued — geographical extent is a security for liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of the militia is incident to common defense and should be national for uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of regulating the militia, and of commanding its services in times of insurrection and invasion are natural incidents to the duties of superintending the common defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity in organization and discipline produces mutual intelligence and concert when militia are called into service; only national direction can accomplish such uniformity. The proposed Constitution empowers the Union 'to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia,' reserving appointment of officers and training authority to states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete disciplining of the entire militia is impracticable and undesirable
rubrics_metrics.description: The project of disciplining all the militia of the United States is as futile as it would be injurious ... To oblige the great body of the yeomanry ... to be under arms ... would be a real grievance ... and a serious public inconvenience and loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of trying to perfect the entire militia, aim to have the people properly armed/equipped and assemble them once or twice a year; adopt a 'well-digested plan' to form a select corps of moderate extent fit for service — a practical substitute for a standing army and a security against one.

rubrics_metrics.name: State appointment of militia officers as safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular States are to have the sole and exclusive appointment of the officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because officers are appointed by states, fears of the federal militia becoming an engine of usurpation are reduced. State appointment secures a preponderating influence of the states over the militia, alleviating concerns about federal misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to require citizen assistance (posse comitatus) follows from Necessary and Proper clause
rubrics_metrics.description: A right to pass all laws necessary and proper to execute its declared powers would include that of requiring the assistance of the citizens to the officers who may be intrusted with the execution of those laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument rebuts objections claiming a lack of power to call out posse comitatus; it would be incoherent to claim both that federal powers are despotic and that they are too weak to require citizen help. The Necessary and Proper clause implies such incidental authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: General power of taxation for national needs (internal and external)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be interwoven, in the frame of the government, a general power of taxation, in one shape or another ... It must embrace a provision for the support of the national civil list; for the payment of the national debts; and, in general, for all those matters which will call for disbursements out of the national treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money is the vital principle of the body politic; a complete power to procure adequate supply is indispensable. Relying solely on external (import duties) revenue or on requisitions from states is inadequate to meet present and future necessities, public debt, military and civil expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power must be proportionate to its object; unlimited power where object is unlimited
rubrics_metrics.description: Every power ought to be commensurate with its object; that there ought to be no limitation of a power destined to effect a purpose which is itself incapable of limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to taxation: where the needs of a nation are potentially unlimited (e.g., war, debt), the power to provide for them should be unconfined. This principle rebuts proposals to reserve internal taxation to states while limiting national taxation to imposts only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on state requisitions undermines national efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: To say that deficiencies may be provided for by requisitions upon the States is on the one hand to acknowledge that this system cannot be depended upon, and on the other hand to depend upon it for every thing beyond a certain limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience shows requisitions lead to weakness, discord, and inability to provide stable public supplies; they would enfeeble the Union and sow seeds of contention between federal head and members. Fiscal independence of the national government is necessary for vigor, stability, credit, and effective administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: National taxation enables borrowing and preserves public credit in war
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of creating new funds upon new objects of taxation, by its own authority, would enable the national government to borrow as far as its necessities might require ... Foreigners, as well as the citizens of America, could then reasonably repose confidence in its engagements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without credible taxation authority, a government would be driven in war to divert funds, undermining credit; borrowing would be limited and expensive. National taxation assures lenders and allows access to loans essential in modern warfare; dependence on state cooperation would make borrowing unrealistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits on maintaining large standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: For a long time to come, it will not be possible to maintain a large army; and as the means of doing this increase, the population and natural strength of the community will proportionably increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extent of military force must be regulated by the resources of the country. The argument suggests fears of a federal army erecting despotism are misplaced because logistical and resource constraints, and the presence of well-trained militia/select corps, check that risk.
